output:
**The house in Glenmore — saying it once**

Úna set this blog up years ago so the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds could keep up with us. I’ve been glad of it more than once. I’m glad of it now, because I’d rather say this once, properly, to everyone, than have it go round in bits on the phone.

I’ve agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore — the old Mulkerrin place, near Oughterard, where Tom grew up. It closes on 15 January 2027.

Some of you already knew. Some of you heard it second-hand, and I’m sorry about that. That’s my fault, and I’ll come to it. But I want to start with the house itself, because that’s what this is about.

**The house**

It was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. Tom died in March 2024. Since then I’ve driven out every fortnight — forty minutes each way — to air it and check the pipes. People say, “Sure it’s only forty minutes,” and it is, going out. It’s the forty back, and the list in your head before you get there. Is the back door swelling? Has a slate gone? Is there water where there shouldn’t be? I know every gate and pothole on that road now. I could drive it in my sleep, and some mornings I nearly have.

I’m not going to dress this up. The house needs work. Ó Flaithearta’s did a roof survey in September. Slates and the back chimney — €38,000. That’s before you touch the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing to sell to anyone anyway. That’s not a leaky tap or a bit of painting. That’s a decision.

I could have gone on patching it. I’m 71, not 51. And last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there twenty minutes before I could get up. I told nobody until now. I don’t know why I’m telling you now, except that it’s the truth and I’d rather you had the whole of it. Since then I’m afraid of being alone at the house. I don’t like the sound of that sentence. It’s still true. I can’t go on maintaining it.

That’s the why of it. There’s no grand plan behind it. It’s not that I’ve stopped caring about the house. It’s that I’ve spent two years caring for it on my own, and I’m tired, and I’m not able for it. I taught primary school for nearly forty years. I know how to put a notice on a board. I should have put this on the board.

I’ve had people ask me why I don’t rent it out. I’ve thought about that too. But renting it means being a landlord at 71, and it means someone else’s family in it while I’m still tied to the pipes and the roof and the septic tank. It doesn’t solve the thing that’s actually wrong, which is that I can’t be out there on my own. It just puts a tenant between me and the problem.

And I know it’s not just my house. It’s Tom’s, and Pádraig’s, and all of yours in some way. That’s why I’m not selling it quietly. That’s why I’m writing this. I don’t expect everyone to agree with me. I do expect to be able to say I told you myself.

**The sale**

The sale was agreed on 3 November with a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They have two small children. They want to live in it — not a holiday let, not an investment, not a weekend place for someone from Dublin. The price was fair. It was under what the Dublin crowd offered in the summer. I took the lower one on purpose. I’m not going to pretend I’m a saint about that. I wanted a family in it. Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve thought about that a lot.

I’ve met Aoife and Kevin. They’re not buying a postcard. They know the roof needs doing. They know the back bedroom is damp. They’re not coming in with notions. They want a home for their children, and I believe them.

I know some of you will have your own views about the price, or the timing, or the couple. That’s all right. You’re entitled. But I’m the one who has been driving out there in the rain to check the pipes, and I’m the one who has to make the call. I’ve made it. I’d rather tell you straight than have you wondering.

**The hard part**
